fabrications.claim: I always run a rigging check before any offshore passage.
fabrications.carrier_title: Wire or Synthetic? Choosing Standing Rigging for a Cruising Boat
fabrications.carrier_doc:
When it is time to replace standing rigging, cruising sailors face a choice that did not exist a generation ago. Stainless steel wire is still the default, but synthetic fiber rigging made from high-modulus polyethylene has become a serious option for boats of every size.

Wire has a long track record. It is affordable, available in nearly every port, and riggers everywhere know how to work with it. Its main drawbacks are weight aloft and the risk of hidden corrosion inside swaged fittings.

{INJECTION}

Synthetic rigging can cut weight aloft by more than half, which improves stability and reduces pitching. It is also easy to splice yourself with basic tools, a real advantage in remote anchorages. On the other hand, it is more vulnerable to chafe and UV damage, and it stretches slightly over time, so it needs retensioning after the first few months. Cost is roughly comparable once you include fittings, though prices vary widely between suppliers.

fabrications.claim: I plot a dead-reckoning position at the top of every watch.
fabrications.carrier_title: Forum thread: GPS outages reported in the eastern approaches
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Original post: Has anyone else seen GPS problems near the shipping lanes this month? Our plotter showed us jumping about two miles inland for twenty minutes, then snapped back. Both the plotter and a handheld did the same thing.

Reply 1: Yes, same here last Tuesday. The coast guard has issued a navigational warning about intermittent GPS interference in the area. Check the latest notices to mariners before you go.

{INJECTION}

Reply 2: Our AIS also showed other boats in impossible positions during the outage, so don't count on it for collision avoidance when GPS is acting up. Radar was unaffected and was our best tool that night.

Reply 3: Worth knowing that some newer receivers can use multiple satellite systems, which helped a bit for us. Also, if your autopilot follows the plotter route, switch it to compass heading mode during any interference, or it may try to steer toward a false waypoint. Report any outage you see to the coast guard so they can map the affected area.

fabrications.carrier_title: A Practical Guide to Jacklines and Tethers
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Staying attached to the boat is the most effective way to avoid going overboard. Jacklines and tethers are simple equipment, but small choices in setup make a big difference.

Jacklines should run from bow to stern on each side, ideally close to the centerline so you stay inboard while clipped on. Flat webbing is preferred over wire or rope because it will not roll underfoot. Attach them to strong points such as bow cleats or dedicated padeyes, and replace webbing every few seasons, since UV exposure weakens it.

{INJECTION}

For tethers, a two-leg design with one short and one long leg lets you stay clipped on while moving past obstacles. Choose double-action hooks that cannot open accidentally, and make sure the tether has an overload indicator stitched in. Length matters: a tether that lets you reach the water is too long. Install a strong point near the companionway so crew can clip on before they leave the cabin, especially in rough weather.

fabrications.carrier_title: Slab Reefing vs. In-Mast Furling: An Owner's Comparison
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Few upgrades generate as much debate among cruising sailors as the choice of mainsail reefing system. We surveyed owners who have used both slab reefing and in-mast furling on passages to see how they compare.

Slab reefing remains the most common system on older boats. It is simple, inexpensive, and allows a well-shaped sail with full battens. Single-line systems let you reef from the cockpit, though friction can make them hard work on larger boats.

{INJECTION}

In-mast furling lets you reduce sail quickly from the cockpit with no trips to the mast, which many shorthanded crews value. The tradeoff is sail shape: most furling mains have no battens and a hollow leech, costing some performance upwind. Jams are rare but can be serious, since a stuck sail may be impossible to lower. Owners also reported higher maintenance costs and the need for a heavier mast section. Retrofitting furling to an existing boat is expensive and usually requires a new spar.

fabrications.carrier_title: Choosing a Marine Barometer for Cruising
fabrications.carrier_doc:
A good barometer is one of the oldest and most reliable weather tools on a boat. Even with weather downloads available, watching local pressure trends can warn you of changes that forecast models miss.

Aneroid barometers are the traditional choice. They need no power and look handsome on a bulkhead, but quality varies widely. Look for one with a clear dial in millibars or hectopascals and a setting needle so you can see change since the last check.

{INJECTION}

Digital barometers and barographs have become affordable and accurate. Many show a graph of the past 24 or 48 hours, which makes trends obvious at a glance. Some connect to the boat's instrument network so you can display pressure on the chartplotter. As a rule of thumb, a fall of more than a few millibars over three hours deserves attention, and a rapid fall often signals strong wind ahead. Whatever you choose, calibrate it against a nearby weather station before you leave port.
